questions: What kind of food do you like to eat?
Do you often cook at home?
Is there any food you disliked as a child but enjoy now?
Do you prefer eating at home or eating out?
Has the way people in your country eat changed in recent years?
tips: Name specific dishes and briefly explain what they are; the examiner may not know local food.
Use sensory adjectives (crispy, tangy, rich, mild) instead of repeating 'delicious'.
For questions about the past, 'used to' and 'would' sound natural for repeated habits.
usefulPhrases: It's a kind of... made with...
I'm not much of a cook, to be honest.
I couldn't stand it when I was younger.
These days I've really developed a taste for...
Eating out has become far more common.

samples.text:
[What kind of food do you like to eat?]
I like spicy food very much, like Padang food. Padang food is from West Sumatra and it is very spicy and have a lot of coconut milk. My favourite is rendang, it is beef which is cook for many hours. It is very delicious.

[Do you often cook at home?]
Not so often, because I am busy with my work. Maybe one or two times in a week I cook, usually simple food like fried rice or noodle. In weekend sometimes I cook with my mother, and she teach me how to make some traditional food.

[Do you prefer eating at home or eating out?]
I prefer eating at home because it is more healthy and more cheap. But sometimes I eat out with my friends, because it is fun.
samples.commentary: Fluency & Coherence: the candidate keeps talking and answers are relevant, but ideas are linked with simple connectors and 'very' and 'delicious' are relied on. Lexical Resource: enough vocabulary to discuss the topic, including some specific items ('coconut milk', 'rendang'), but comparatives are wrongly formed ('more cheap', 'more healthy'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy: subject-verb agreement and passive errors ('have a lot of', 'which is cook') recur, though meaning is clear. Pronunciation: the repetitive 'it is...' sentence frames suggest an even, syllable-timed rhythm with limited chunking, though this would generally be intelligible.

samples.text:
[What kind of food do you like to eat?]
I'm a big fan of anything spicy, particularly Padang cooking from West Sumatra. My all-time favourite is rendang, which is beef slow-cooked in coconut milk and spices until it's almost dry. It takes hours to make, which is why it's usually served at special occasions.

[Do you often cook at home?]
Not as much as I'd like. During the week I tend to grab something quick on the way home, but at weekends I sometimes help my mum in the kitchen. She's been trying to teach me her version of rendang, although I haven't quite mastered it yet.

[Is there any food you disliked as a child but enjoy now?]
Bitter gourd, definitely. I used to refuse to eat it, but now I actually quite like the bitterness, especially when it's stir-fried with egg.
samples.commentary: Fluency & Coherence: answers are extended fluently, with clear explanation and appropriate use of connectives ('which is why', 'although'). Lexical Resource: precise, topic-specific vocabulary ('slow-cooked', 'stir-fried', 'bitter gourd') and idiomatic phrases ('all-time favourite', 'grab something quick') are used appropriately. Grammatical Range & Accuracy: a good mix of relative clauses, present perfect continuous and 'used to', largely error-free. Pronunciation: the phrasing suggests natural chunking ('slow-cooked in coconut milk and spices'), although the answers are slightly more predictable in rhythm than those at band 8.

samples.text:
[Is there any food you disliked as a child but enjoy now?]
Bitter gourd, without a doubt. As a kid I'd do anything to avoid it; I used to hide it under my rice. But somewhere along the way I developed a taste for that sharp, almost medicinal bitterness, and now I'll actually order it if I see it on a menu.

[Do you prefer eating at home or eating out?]
It really depends on what I'm after. If I want comfort food, nothing beats my mother's cooking. But eating out is more of a social thing for me, a chance to catch up with friends, so the food itself is almost secondary.

[Has the way people in your country eat changed in recent years?]
Enormously. Food delivery apps have made it almost effortless to order in, so a lot of younger people in the cities barely cook at all. There's also been a noticeable shift towards international food. Korean and Japanese restaurants have popped up everywhere, which would have been unthinkable twenty years ago.
samples.commentary: Fluency & Coherence: the candidate speaks effortlessly and develops each answer with relevant, well-organised detail. Lexical Resource: sophisticated, idiomatic choices ('developed a taste for', 'almost medicinal bitterness', 'nothing beats', 'popped up everywhere') are used naturally and precisely. Grammatical Range & Accuracy: wide range, including 'would' for past habits, conditionals and complex noun phrases, with no evident errors. Pronunciation: short emphatic answers ('Enormously.', 'Bitter gourd, without a doubt.') followed by longer explanations show control of rhythm and stress that would make the speech engaging to listen to.
